subject: CRS
category: Formation and Composition of the Old Testament
question: List at least twenty (20) books of the Old Testament as they appear in the Revised Standard Version
modelAnswer:
The Revised Standard Version (RSV) has 39 Old Testament books, in this order (any twenty in the correct order earn the marks):
1. Genesis
2. Exodus
3. Leviticus
4. Numbers
5. Deuteronomy
6. Joshua
7. Judges
8. Ruth
9. 1 Samuel
10. 2 Samuel
11. 1 Kings
12. 2 Kings
13. 1 Chronicles
14. 2 Chronicles
15. Ezra
16. Nehemiah
17. Esther
18. Job
19. Psalms
20. Proverbs
21. Ecclesiastes
22. Song of Solomon
23. Isaiah
24. Jeremiah
25. Lamentations
26. Ezekiel
27. Daniel
28. Hosea
29. Joel
30. Amos
31. Obadiah
32. Jonah
33. Micah
34. Nahum
35. Habakkuk
36. Zephaniah
37. Haggai
38. Zechariah
39. Malachi

The books fall into groups: the Pentateuch or Law (Genesis–Deuteronomy), the Historical Books (Joshua–Esther), the Poetic/Wisdom Books (Job–Song of Solomon), the Major Prophets (Isaiah–Daniel) and the Minor Prophets (Hosea–Malachi). Note that 1 and 2 Samuel, 1 and 2 Kings and 1 and 2 Chronicles each count as two separate books.

subject: CRS
category: Formation and Composition of the Old Testament
question: Define inspiration and briefly explain its views or theories
modelAnswer:
Definition: inspiration is the belief that God guided the human writers of Scripture by His Spirit, so that what they wrote is the Word of God. The term comes from 2 Timothy 3:16, where Scripture is described as 'inspired by God' (Greek theopneustos, 'God-breathed'); 2 Peter 1:21 says the writers 'spoke from God as they were moved by the Holy Spirit'.

Views (theories) of inspiration:
1. Mechanical (dictation) theory: God dictated the words and the writers were passive instruments, like secretaries or pens. Criticism: it ignores the clear differences in style, vocabulary and personality among the writers.
2. Verbal plenary theory: every word (verbal) and every part (plenary) of Scripture is inspired, yet God used the writers' own personalities, styles and knowledge. This is the traditional evangelical view.
3. Dynamic theory: God inspired the writers' thoughts and the message, but left them free to choose their own words. The ideas are divine; the words are human.
4. Natural (intuition) theory: the writers were gifted religious geniuses, inspired in the same way as great poets or thinkers. Criticism: it makes the Bible no different from other great literature.
5. Illumination theory: the Holy Spirit heightened the writers' normal religious insight, as He enlightens all believers, but only in degree, not in kind.
6. Partial (concept) theory: only some parts of the Bible (e.g. matters of faith and morals) are inspired, not historical or scientific details.
7. Neo-orthodox (encounter) view: the Bible becomes the Word of God when God speaks to a reader through it.

These views differ on whether inspiration applies to the words, the thoughts or the writers, and on how far the human element was involved.

subject: CRS
question: Examine the objections against Mosaic authorship of the Pentateuch
modelAnswer:
Traditionally, Jews and Christians held that Moses wrote the Pentateuch (Genesis–Deuteronomy). Modern critical scholars raised these objections:
1. The account of Moses' death and burial (Deuteronomy 34:5–12): Moses could not have recorded his own death, and the text says 'no man knows the place of his burial to this day', implying a later writer.
2. Third-person references to Moses: Moses is usually spoken of as 'he', and Numbers 12:3 calls him 'very meek, more than all men', which a humble man would hardly write about himself.
3. Anachronisms: statements that suit a later time, e.g. 'the Canaanites were then in the land' (Genesis 12:6; 13:7), kings who reigned in Edom 'before any king reigned over Israel' (Genesis 36:31), the city named Dan (Genesis 14:14) though it was so named only in Judges 18:29, and phrases like 'to this day'.
4. Different names for God: the use of Yahweh (LORD) in some passages and Elohim (God) in others suggests different sources.
5. Duplicate or parallel accounts (doublets): two creation accounts (Genesis 1 and 2), two flood traditions, two accounts of the naming of Beersheba, and the patriarch passing off his wife as his sister three times.
6. Differences in style, vocabulary and theology between sections (e.g. the priestly lists in Leviticus and Numbers compared with the narrative style elsewhere).
7. The Documentary Hypothesis (Graf–Wellhausen): on these grounds scholars proposed four sources, J (Yahwist, c. 950 BC), E (Elohist, c. 850 BC), D (Deuteronomist, c. 621 BC, linked with Josiah's reform) and P (Priestly, c. 500 BC), combined by later editors.
8. Moses is said to have written only certain parts (e.g. Exodus 17:14; 24:4; Deuteronomy 31:9), not the whole.

Defenders of Mosaic authorship reply that Joshua or another writer added the account of Moses' death, that later scribes updated place names, and that different names for God reflect different aspects of His nature rather than different authors.

subject: CRS
category: The Rise of Monarchy in Israel
question: Discuss the role of Samuel as a judge in Israel
modelAnswer:
Samuel was the last of the judges and also a prophet and priest (1 Samuel 1–12). His role as judge included:
1. Administering justice: he judged Israel all the days of his life, going on a yearly circuit to Bethel, Gilgal and Mizpah and returning to his home at Ramah, where he also judged the people and built an altar (1 Samuel 7:15–17).
2. Spiritual leadership and revival: at Mizpah he called Israel to put away the foreign gods (the Baals and Ashtaroth), to return to the Lord with all their heart and to serve Him only; the people fasted and confessed their sin (1 Samuel 7:3–6).
3. Intercessor: he prayed for Israel and offered a sacrifice to the Lord for them; he promised, 'Far be it from me that I should sin against the Lord by ceasing to pray for you' (1 Samuel 12:23).
4. Military deliverer: when the Philistines attacked at Mizpah, Samuel offered a sacrifice and cried to the Lord; the Lord thundered and the Philistines were routed. He set up a stone called Ebenezer ('Hitherto the Lord has helped us'). The Philistines were subdued and the cities they had taken were restored (1 Samuel 7:7–14).
5. Peace-maker: there was peace between Israel and the Amorites during his time.
6. Kingmaker and link to the monarchy: when the people asked for a king, he warned them of the ways of a king, then anointed Saul (1 Samuel 8–10) and later David (1 Samuel 16), and presented the 'rights and duties of the kingship' to the people.
7. Example of integrity: in his farewell speech at Gilgal he challenged the people to name anyone he had cheated, oppressed or taken a bribe from, and they testified that he had not (1 Samuel 12:3–5).

Weakness: he appointed his sons Joel and Abijah as judges in Beersheba, but they took bribes and perverted justice, which was one reason the elders asked for a king (1 Samuel 8:1–5).

subject: CRS
category: The Rise of Monarchy in Israel
question: Highlight the implications of King Saul's inauguration at Gilgal for Nigerian leaders
modelAnswer:
Background (1 Samuel 11:12–12:25): after Saul defeated the Ammonites at Jabesh-gilead, Samuel called the people to Gilgal to 'renew the kingdom'. There they made Saul king before the Lord, offered peace offerings and rejoiced. Saul refused to punish those who had despised him earlier, saying 'Not a man shall be put to death this day, for today the Lord has wrought deliverance in Israel'. Samuel then gave his farewell speech, defending his integrity, reminding the people of God's past deliverances, warning that both king and people must fear and obey the Lord, and calling down thunder and rain at wheat harvest as a sign of their sin in asking for a king.

Implications for Nigerian leaders:
1. Leadership is from God: Saul was made king 'before the Lord'; leaders should see their office as a trust from God and rule with the fear of God.
2. Obedience to God and the law: Samuel warned that if king and people obeyed God, all would be well, but if they rebelled, God's hand would be against them; leaders must obey God's will and the constitution.
3. Magnanimity and reconciliation: Saul forgave those who had opposed him; Nigerian leaders should avoid vengeance against political opponents after elections and promote unity.
4. Giving glory to God for victory: Saul attributed the victory to the Lord, not himself; leaders should be humble and not arrogant in success.
5. Accountability and integrity: Samuel publicly challenged the people to accuse him of fraud, oppression or bribery; leaders should keep clean records and be ready to give account of their stewardship.
6. Popular acceptance and legitimacy: all the people took part in making Saul king; leaders should come to power with the genuine consent of the people through credible elections.
7. Respect for spiritual and moral counsel: Saul was installed through the prophet; leaders should listen to good advice and moral voices.
8. Warning of failure: Saul later disobeyed God and was rejected (1 Samuel 13 and 15); a good beginning must be followed by continued faithfulness, or leadership will fail.

subject: CRS
category: The Rise of Prophecy in Israel
question: Examine the contributions of Prophet Elisha to the nation of Israel during the period of famine
modelAnswer:
Elisha, the successor of Elijah, ministered in the Northern Kingdom of Israel in the 9th century BC. His contributions during periods of famine included:
1. Purifying the poisoned pottage (2 Kings 4:38–41): when there was a famine in Gilgal, a pot of stew was poisoned by wild gourds; Elisha threw meal into the pot and it became harmless, saving the sons of the prophets.
2. Feeding a hundred men (2 Kings 4:42–44): a man brought twenty loaves of barley and fresh grain; Elisha told his servant to feed a hundred men with it, and they ate and had some left over, as the Lord had said.
3. Warning the Shunammite woman (2 Kings 8:1–6): Elisha told her to leave the land because the Lord had called for a seven-year famine; she went to the land of the Philistines and was preserved, and on her return the king restored her house and land because of Elisha's testimony.
4. Prophecy of relief during the siege of Samaria (2 Kings 6:24–7:20): when Ben-hadad of Syria besieged Samaria, the famine was so severe that a donkey's head sold for eighty shekels and mothers ate their children. The king blamed Elisha, but Elisha prophesied that by the next day fine meal and barley would sell cheaply at the gate of Samaria. The Lord made the Syrians hear the sound of a great army and they fled; four lepers discovered the empty camp and the people plundered it, fulfilling the prophecy. The officer who doubted died, trampled at the gate.
5. Providing water for the armies (2 Kings 3:16–20): during the campaign against Moab, the armies of Israel, Judah and Edom had no water; Elisha told them to dig trenches, which filled with water without rain.
6. Spiritual leadership: through these acts Elisha showed that the Lord, not Baal, controlled rain, food and life, encouraged faith in God and confronted the kings' unbelief.

Note: other miracles of Elisha (e.g. multiplying the widow's oil to pay her debt, 2 Kings 4:1–7, and healing Naaman, 2 Kings 5) are not directly linked to famine.

subject: CRS
category: The Rise of Prophecy in Israel
question: Examine the call and commission of Prophet Isaiah
modelAnswer:
Isaiah's call is recorded in Isaiah 6, 'in the year that King Uzziah died' (about 740 BC).
1. The vision: Isaiah saw the Lord sitting upon a high and lofty throne, with His train filling the temple. Above Him stood seraphim, each with six wings: two covered the face, two covered the feet and two were used for flying.
2. The song of the seraphim: they called to one another, 'Holy, holy, holy is the Lord of hosts; the whole earth is full of His glory'. The foundations shook and the house was filled with smoke.
3. Isaiah's confession: 'Woe is me! For I am lost; for I am a man of unclean lips, and I dwell in the midst of a people of unclean lips; for my eyes have seen the King, the Lord of hosts.' He recognised his own sinfulness and that of the nation.
4. Cleansing: one of the seraphim took a burning coal from the altar with tongs and touched his mouth, saying, 'Behold, this has touched your lips; your guilt is taken away, and your sin forgiven.'
5. The call: the Lord asked, 'Whom shall I send, and who will go for us?' Isaiah answered, 'Here am I! Send me.'
6. The commission: he was sent to tell the people, 'Hear and hear, but do not understand; see and see, but do not perceive', to make their hearts fat, their ears heavy and their eyes shut, lest they turn and be healed. His preaching would harden a rebellious people.
7. Duration and outcome: when Isaiah asked 'How long, O Lord?', he was told: until cities lie waste, houses are empty and the land is desolate, and the Lord removes the people far away (exile). Yet a holy seed would remain, like the stump of a felled tree (a remnant).

Significance: the holiness of God; the need for confession and cleansing before service; God's initiative and the prophet's willing response; the hard message of judgment combined with hope through the remnant.

subject: CRS
category: The Rise of Prophecy in Israel
question: Discuss God's charges against Israel's neighbours according to Prophet Amos.
modelAnswer:
In Amos 1:3–2:3 God pronounces judgment, using the formula 'For three transgressions of ... and for four, I will not revoke the punishment', on six neighbouring nations:
1. Damascus (Syria/Aram) (1:3–5): they 'threshed Gilead with threshing sledges of iron', i.e. treated the people of Gilead with extreme cruelty in war. Punishment: fire on the house of Hazael and the strongholds of Ben-hadad; the people would go into exile to Kir.
2. Gaza (Philistia) (1:6–8): they carried a whole people into exile to deliver them up to Edom, i.e. slave trading. Punishment: fire on the walls of Gaza; Ashdod, Ashkelon and Ekron would also perish.
3. Tyre (Phoenicia) (1:9–10): they delivered a whole people to Edom as slaves and 'did not remember the covenant of brotherhood' (broke a treaty). Punishment: fire on the walls of Tyre.
4. Edom (1:11–12): he pursued his brother (Israel) with the sword, cast off all pity, and kept his anger and wrath for ever (unforgiving hatred and revenge). Punishment: fire on Teman and the strongholds of Bozrah.
5. Ammon (1:13–15): they ripped up women with child in Gilead in order to enlarge their border (brutal war crimes for territory). Punishment: fire on Rabbah; their king would go into exile.
6. Moab (2:1–3): he burned to lime the bones of the king of Edom (desecration of the dead). Punishment: fire on Kerioth; Moab would die amid uproar and its ruler would be cut off.

Lessons: God is the Lord of all nations, not of Israel alone; He judges crimes against humanity (cruelty, slavery, treaty-breaking, hatred, atrocities, desecration) even by nations that do not have His law; the same principle then led to His charges against Judah and Israel (2:4–16).
